riB[s11nXTxmG)ku_y:).text: "Scroll X & Y" hold the horizontal and vertical distance that a level is current scrolled                  to right now.  It is a global variable (all sprites can see it)."Next Scr X & Y" hold the location the level will be scrolled to when it is next re-drawn (Having a current and next scroll x & y allows us to position our sprites to be drawn lined up with the level where it will be next, but check for collisions with where it is now)."Player X & Y" hold the position of the player"Speed X & Y" hold the players momentum (speed)"Can Jump?" must be greater than 0 for the player to be able to jump.

Ww^~~#:EebL:R(Y@UEfx.text: This is our game loop where we loop around forever:* First dealing with "The Player".* Then broadcasting to all the other sprites to update themselves.Having a loop with the last block as a bloadcast & wait is VERY purposful and a method I have adopted since scripting paper minecraft.  The reason is that without the 'and wait' the other sprites might not finish updating before the this loop starts again (and that can make your game unstable). But if you do a 'broadcast and wait' anywhere but the end of the loop then the 'and wait' imposes an extra 1/30th of a second delay in to your game which halfs the frame rate and makes it run slower and jerkier.

jR^oVradS[0aYc+upN5|.text: Each time 'The Player' loops around it's main game loop, it will broadcast a 'tick' event which triggers here in each of the 'Level' sprite clones.As we are now moving this background sprite, we set the 'Scroll X & Y' to the value of 'Next Scr X & Y'... This iensures the 'Scroll X & Y' only ever holds the current position of the scrolling level (this is important for collision checks)We Set the position of this Level sprite to it's position (Offset) minus of the Scroll X & Y.

Fi|kM.5NblowEU6U5wjU.text: Each time 'The Player' loops around it's main game loop, it will broadcast a 'tick' event which triggers here in each of the 'Level' sprite clones.We Set the position to this Level sprite based on it's Offset and HALF of the Scroll X & Y set by 'The Player' before it triggered this event.Here you see I have created a 'Looping X' variable to work out the X position of the background.  Note especially how I have used the 'mod' block?  This is a really useful mathematical block in programming.  It's full name is 'modulas' and it gives you 'the remainder after dividing a number by the second argument).  So 6 mod 5 = 1 (because after dividing 6 by 5 we have 1 left over).  The reason this is so useful is that the remainder is always between 0 and the second argument (take away one).  It is worth experimenting with, but it allows us to make a sprite appear to move across the screen and then suddenly loop back to the other side and continue in the same direction over and over again, which is perfect for the background sprites.

7Ps:bD6H{Ig/eYvJt#.=.text: The parallax background is a single background cloned to two backgrounds next to each other, and the second one is flipped around (mirrored) to make it a repeating pattern.Notice I offset each tile by 478 pixels.  A full screen is actually 480 pixels, but by reducing it by 2 pixels you remove any gap that can appear due to scratch scaling the project up to full screen size.
